paper_identity.paper_title: Risks in rainfed agriculture and adaptation strategies in India: Profile and socio-economic correlates

paper_summary: A primary household survey of 207 cotton-growing farmers in Jalgaon and Yavatmal districts of Maharashtra (2015) profiles farmer-perceived risks (weather, inputs, services, credit, information, output price) and the ex-ante and ex-post adaptation strategies they use. Composite ex-ante and ex-post adaptation indices (0-1) are constructed and regressed (beta regression) on socio-economic covariates: caste, tenancy, operational holding, share of irrigated area, distance to market, KCC ownership, association membership, value of land owned, and risk attitude (PCA). Drought, late monsoon, untimely rainfall, groundwater unreliability, high input prices, pesticide pressure on Bt cotton, and high cotton price volatility coupled with weak MSP/insurance institutions emerge as the dominant risks shaping rainfed adaptation behaviour.
study_region: Maharashtra, India - Jalgaon district (Khandesh region; tehsils Jamner, Parola) and Yavatmal district (Vidarbha region; tehsils Ghatanji, Kelapur); 24 villages; 207 cotton farmers analysed
study_period: Primary survey conducted July-September 2015; references to cotton sector trends 1978-79 to 2016
methodology: Multi-stage random household survey with face-to-face Likert-scale questionnaires and FGDs; descriptive statistics on perceived risk and adoption shares; composite ex-ante (11 strategies) and ex-post (50 strategies) adaptation indices (0-1); beta regression (logit link) for index covariates with marginal effects
paper_type_rationale: Empirical case study using primary survey data and beta regression of an adaptation index on socio-economic covariates in two cotton districts of Maharashtra; it descriptively profiles risks and statistically tests covariates rather than building a fully specified end-to-end mechanism model.

mapping_notes: The paper's core analytical objects are two composite indices (ex-ante and ex-post) and their socio-economic covariates from a beta regression. Most covariates (caste, tenancy, distance to market, KCC, association membership, owned-land value, risk-attitude PCA) do not have direct base-taxonomy parents and are kept as new variables aligned with the existing taxonomy-expansion namespace where possible (NEW_institutional_credit_access, NEW_farmer_organization_membership, NEW_land_holding_size, etc.). Drought / late-monsoon / temperature-variation risks are mapped to closest base-taxonomy parents (drought_freq, drysp_4w_trend, NEW_land_surface_temp_trend). Cotton-specific variables (output-price volatility, MSP coverage gap, pesticide use intensity, input-supply quality) are introduced as new variables since they are central to rainfed cotton risk but not in current taxonomy.
limitations: Findings are based on a 2015 cross-section of 207 cotton farmers in two Maharashtra districts (Jalgaon, Yavatmal) and may not generalize to other rainfed crops or regions. Variables are largely Likert-derived farmer-reported scores rather than directly measured biophysical / economic quantities, so transferability to remote-sensing- or census-based district indicators requires alignment of definitions. Coefficients for KCC and association membership show counterintuitive signs reflecting weak local KCC delivery rather than universal causal impact - these should be interpreted as study-specific. The paper does not report rainfall, groundwater depth, or yield measurements directly; biophysical variables are inferred from descriptive narrative.

important_variables_narrative: The paper's mechanism story has three pillars. (i) On the biophysical side, drought_freq (91.3% farmer agreement), late-monsoon dry spells and high temperature variation are the dominant rainfall-side drivers of cotton yield risk, transmitted through compensatory groundwater pumping (irrigation_demand → g_annual_trend → well_depth / NEW_irrigation_water_supply_reliability / NEW_energy_cost_pumping). (ii) On the institutional / market side, NEW_msp_coverage_gap and weak NEW_crop_insurance_adoption push exposure into NEW_output_price_volatility and into self-insurance via NEW_livestock_mortality and NEW_non_farm_income_availability. (iii) On the social / household side, the beta-regression results identify NEW_caste_disadvantage, NEW_tenancy_share, NEW_land_holding_size, irrigated_area_fraction, NEW_owned_land_value, NEW_market_access_distance and NEW_farmer_risk_perception_index as the most explanatory correlates of the two adaptation indices, with caste emerging as the single strongest determinant of both ex-ante and ex-post coping capacity. These three pillars together provide a tractable cross-stressor map - drought → groundwater → irrigation_challenges → rainfed_risk - while also identifying clear socio-economic levers (tenancy, caste-based targeting, market access, insurance/MSP coverage) for policy.
